extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers writing academic research reports (new researchers/advanced undergraduates/graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing, testing, and defending warrants in academic arguments and for planning/drafting research reports (when to state warrants, how to challenge them, and how to plan introductions/outlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a warrant (When X, then Y)
rubrics_metrics.description: A warrant consists of two parts: (i) a general circumstance that lets us draw a conclusion and (ii) a general consequence. For clarity, warrants should be stated in the explicit two-part form 'When X, then Y.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any compressed warrant can be deconstructed into a general circumstance and consequence and then aligned with a specific reason and specific claim (example: When a nation's labor force shrinks, its economic future is grim → Russia's birthrate is low and life expectancy fell → Therefore its economic future is grim). Always check that the specific reason and claim are instances of the general parts of the warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic warrants are community-specific and often unstated
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic warrants are specific principles of reasoning developed within research communities and are countless; advanced researchers usually omit stating them because they assume readers know them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners must learn which warrants a field takes for granted and may need to state warrants when writing for non-experts or when a warrant would seem controversial or unfamiliar to readers in another community. Experts sometimes compress warrants into single statements ('Shared DNA is the measure of the relationship between species'); for clarity, deconstruct compressed warrants when teaching or communicating across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the warrant basically true?
rubrics_metrics.description: A warrant must be basically true; if readers think a warrant is false, good reasons and evidence for the claim will not suffice to persuade them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When readers may doubt the warrant, treat the warrant itself as a claim needing its own reasons and evidence (cite studies, examples, or authorities that confirm it). Provide direct evidence or argumentation to support the warrant before using it to connect reason and claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is your warrant prudently limited?
rubrics_metrics.description: A warrant can be true but valid only within limits; blanket statements are often too broad and invite skepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualify warrants prudently (use 'most', 'usually', etc.) but then show that exceptions do not undercut your specific reason and claim—define frequency or conditions or explain why exceptions don't apply in your case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Can your warrant be trumped by a competing warrant?
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple plausible warrants may point to conflicting inferences; you must decide which warrant should prevail and defend that choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize competing warrants (e.g., 'Out of sight, out of mind' vs. 'Absence makes the heart grow fonder') and provide an argument or evidence that gives priority to your chosen warrant over alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is your warrant appropriate to your readers' community?
rubrics_metrics.description: Even true and well-limited warrants may be rejected if they conflict with the standards or assumptions of the readers' research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt warrants to the conventions of the discipline (legal, scientific, humanistic). If a warrant is new or counterintuitive in the community, explicitly justify it by citing others in the field who use it or by defending it on disciplinary grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are the specific reason and claim good instances of the general warrant?
rubrics_metrics.description: You must ensure your specific reason and claim are valid instances of the general circumstance and consequence asserted by the warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose mismatches by aligning general circumstance → specific reason and general consequence → specific claim (examples: Ahmed/Anya gun argument; TV violence argument). If not valid instances, revise the reason or the warrant so the specific evidence properly falls under the warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to state a warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: State an explicit warrant when necessary in these three occasions: (1) readers are outside your field; (2) you use a principle of reasoning that is new or controversial in your field; (3) you make a claim readers will resist because they don't want it to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers are non-experts, define the warrant they won't know. If the warrant is controversial, state it and justify it by showing others who use it. If the claim is emotionally or ideologically resisted, begin by establishing a warrant readers are likely to accept before presenting the reason and claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging warrants based on experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants grounded in experience or reports (e.g., 'When people habitually lie, we don't trust them') can be challenged on the reliability of experience or by finding counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either question the reliability of the reported experience (difficult) or present robust counterexamples that cannot be dismissed as special cases; choose the counterexample strategy when you have good cases to show exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging warrants based on authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants backed by authority ('When authority X says Y, Y must be so') are difficult to overturn but can be attacked by questioning the authority's expertise or completeness of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The least aggressive method: show the authority lacks full evidence or has exceeded expertise. The aggressive method: argue the source is not an authority on the matter. Provide alternative credible sources or show gaps in the authority's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging warrants based on systems of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants supported by systems (definitions, principles, theories in math, biology, law) rest on broader frameworks rather than isolated facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To challenge these warrants you must either dispute the underlying system (hard) or show the particular case does not fall under that system—demonstrate boundary conditions or exceptions that exclude your case from the warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging general cultural warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants grounded in broad cultural common sense (e.g., 'Out of sight, out of mind') are resilient and tied to cultural heritage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers will resist challenges; change is slow. You can still challenge them, but expect strong pushback and the need for persuasive counter-examples, historical/contextual argument, or reinterpretation of cultural meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging methodological warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological 'meta-warrants' (generalization, analogy, sign) are patterns of thought used to infer new cases from known ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical objections exist, but in practical argumentation focus on limiting conditions: show when the methodology applies and when it fails (e.g., analogies fail 'if ...'), point out necessary qualifications, or supply additional evidence to shore up the method's applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging warrants based on articles of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Some warrants are statements of faith or revealed truth and are impervious to rational challenge (e.g., 'When a claim is experienced as revealed truth, it must be true').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often pointless to argue these on rational grounds; either ignore them in empirical inquiry or treat them as subjects for interpretive or theological inquiry rather than evidence-based debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of arguments (evidence-based vs. warrant-inferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish (1) arguments that back up a claim with reasons based on evidence and (2) arguments that infer a claim from a reason plus a warrant; researchers trust the first kind more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, back reasons with hard evidence. Arguments that rely solely on broad unqualified warrants are seen as ideological; if you must use a warrant-based argument, also provide supporting empirical evidence for the reason to avoid shakiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness to plan a draft (what you should know before drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: You are ready to draft when you know: who your readers are and why they should care; the ethos you want to project; a two- to three-sentence sketch of your question and answer; reasons and evidence that support your claim; likely questions/alternatives/objections and responses; and when readers may not see the relevance of a reason to a claim and what warrant connects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep writing summaries, analyses, and critiques from the start so you can sketch your plan early; begin drafting only when you can meet these conditions and leave time for revision because early drafting often produces material that will be discarded or reorganized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid three common but flawed plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not: (i) organize your report as a narrative of your thinking (a chronology of how you thought or discovered things); (ii) assemble your report as a patchwork of your sources (quilting); (iii) map your report directly onto the language or order of your assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect the first problem by highlighting sentences about how you thought or what you did; avoid quilting by providing analysis rather than stitched summaries; and if the assignment lists issues, do not follow their order slavishly—reorganize topics conceptually to serve your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional experimental sciences report structure (IMRD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fields, especially experimental sciences, expect reports to follow the conventional plan: Introduction - Methods and Materials - Results - Discussion - Conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your field requires a conventional plan, ask instructors or find a model; in many fields you may create your own plan but must still help readers find what they look for—adhere to disciplinary expectations where they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlining and storyboarding: topic-based vs point-based outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: A topic-based outline (nouns/phrases) works for short papers if you already know the point for each section. For longer papers, point-based outlines (explicit points) are more useful. A storyboard places each main point on a separate movable page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A point outline helps test whether your argument hangs together; avoid formal, rigid outlines that lock you into a final form too soon. Use storyboards to move pages around physically, group related pages, and get a visual 'picture' of the project's organization and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch a working introduction (four parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A working introduction should sketch: (1) a brief summary of only the key points in only the most relevant sources (ordered usefully); (2) rephrase the question as a flaw or gap in those sources; (3) sketch an answer to 'So what if we don't find out?'; (4) state the answer as your point or promise an answer in a launching point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You will likely write the introduction twice (a sketch for yourself and a final version for readers). Decide whether to state your main point at the end of the introduction (gives readers control and clarity) or wait until the conclusion (creates a more controlling narrative). Most readers prefer the point stated in the introduction; doing so also helps you stay on track while writing.
